source.title: Comparing the effectiveness of top-down and bottom-up activation steering for bypassing refusal on harmful prompts

record.file_problem: The text appears complete, but the appendix figure itself is not rendered in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: Applies the harmful-minus-harmless mean activation direction and subtracts its projected component during inference, then evaluates harmful responses on a new chat model.
record.gate_note: The study reports comparative steering outcomes but the supplied text does not include the appendix figure's underlying scores. It also mentions results from prior work; those are not recorded as this study's findings. The figure caption and outcome statements do not disaggregate the hybrid results between hybrid and hybrid2.
record.test_reason: The study applies the Arditi et al. difference-in-means direction to Qwen1.5-0.5B-Chat with AdvBench/Alpaca prompts. It subtracts the direction's projection at every layer and scores harmful responses with HarmBench. That is a T1-style ablation. In the text, though, results are only relative comparisons between steering methods, with no absolute refusal or compliance rate. The rows therefore cannot show whether ablation removes refusal, and no verdict can be given.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Top-down (difference-in-means) steering is simplest and most robust for bypassing refusal on Qwen1.5-0.5B, and SAE-based steering is less effective and harder to tune. A hybrid beats both at a small benign-capability cost. The authors stress limited hyperparameter tuning and a single small model, and call for broader evaluation.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the harmful-minus-harmless residual mean difference and subtracts its normalized projection across layers, with the last token position chosen for direction extraction. It evaluates Qwen 1.5 500M and also tests SAE-based and hybrid variants.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported comparison depends on the evaluation measure: SAE-reconstructed directions are said to do better with string matching but poorly on HarmBench. The authors also say larger steering coefficients can reduce refusals while degrading benign performance, while small coefficients are ineffective; temperature sampling somewhat mitigates the bottom-up performance penalty. Layer and coefficient sweeps were limited.

fits_no_version.finding: On Qwen1.5-0.5B-Chat, steering with the difference-in-means direction elicits more HarmBench-classified harmful responses than SAE single-feature steering (93% relative). Under a string-matching refusal heuristic, an SAE-reconstructed direction ranks higher instead.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For bypassing refusal, the top-down difference-in-means direction is more effective than bottom-up SAE feature steering, but the ranking depends on the evaluation metric (HarmBench vs string matching).

fits_no_version.finding: A hybrid of direction subtraction plus SAE harmful-feature addition elicits more harmful responses than direction subtraction alone, with a small cost to benign capability.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Combining refusal-direction ablation with SAE feature steering increases harmful compliance beyond ablation alone.

record.peer_reviewed: LessWrong post; peer-review status not stated
record.problems: Only one relatively small model (Qwen 1.5 500M) is tested; hyperparameter tuning and evaluation breadth are limited. The supplied text gives relative comparisons and qualitative capability outcomes, not absolute scores or uncertainty estimates, and the referenced appendix figure is absent.
record.rows_left_out: No figure-only rows were created because the supplied text contains only the appendix caption, not the figure values. The text's general statement that other SAE-based approaches generally performed poorly is not separately itemized because it does not give a distinct, sufficiently specified condition or outcome beyond the SAE result recorded in r5.

untested.parts: Not tested: adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts; an absolute refusal or compliance rate after ablation compared with the unsteered model; capability preservation under ablation alone (benign cost is reported only for the hybrid).
No weight edit or abliteration of released models.
No jailbreak mechanism analysis or adversarial training.
No test of multi-direction or cone geometry.
Harmfulness judgment and refusal decision are not separated.
Single model; no transfer across languages or model variants.

missing.what: The headline figure: average number of AdvBench harmful prompts given harmful responses (HarmBench classifier), per method including top_down and an unsteered baseline if shown. Absolute counts are needed to judge whether ablation removes refusal.
Appendix scores: average number of prompts not refused (refusal-word matching) on harmful and harmless instructions, per steering method. The harmless-prompt counts bear on side effects of ablation.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict is given: every number in the text compares steering methods against each other, never against an unsteered baseline, so V1's claim that ablation removes refusal cannot be checked from the rows. The figures holding absolute counts are not rendered. The relative numbers conflict internally: 35% vs 36% vs '~1.85x' for hybrid over top-down. The paper is a short LessWrong course project with no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: Tests subtraction of a difference-in-means direction and harmful-response outcomes, but does not report adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless requests. It does not establish that removal eliminates refusal, and the general-capability result is only stated for the hybrid approach.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
Tests a deliberate activation intervention, not whether jailbreaks work by suppressing the direction or whether training against ablation adds robustness.

The hybrid combines a refusal-direction intervention with an SAE feature intervention, but the study does not test a geometric account of refusal or whether refusal is represented by multiple directions.
Does not separate harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
Only one model and no language or model-variant transfer are tested.
Does not vary refusal training or training stage.

rows.subject: Qwen 1.5 500M
rows.operation_detail: Subtracts the normalized projected harmful-minus-harmless mean activation direction at every layer during inference.

conditions.value: Harmful prompts; AdvBench used to form the harmful prompt batch

rows.measure: Relative effectiveness at producing harmful responses / bypassing refusal, classified using HarmBench.
rows.value: 93% relative improvement over bottom-up (also described as about 1.93 times as effective).
rows.note: The text reports a relative comparison, not the absolute refusal or compliance rate; it does not show that most or all refusals were removed.
rows.check: The value is a 93% relative improvement of top-down ablation over bottom-up SAE steering. That is a comparison between methods, not a refusal rate against an unsteered baseline, so it cannot show whether refusal was removed. 'Partial' is unsupported, and the baseline should be the unsteered model, which the text does not report.

rows.subject: Qwen 1.5 500M
rows.operation_detail: Combines subtraction of the refusal direction with addition of an SAE harmful-feature decoder direction; hybrid variants are not reported separately.

conditions.value: Evaluation prompts; exact split not stated
Hybrid or hybrid2; results not disaggregated

rows.measure: Relative effectiveness at eliciting harmful responses compared with top-down steering.
rows.value: About 35% relative improvement compared with top-down.
rows.note: The combined intervention does not isolate the causal contribution of the difference-in-means direction.
rows.check: This is a combined intervention (direction subtraction plus SAE feature addition) compared with top-down steering. It is a method comparison and does not isolate the direction. The text gives 35% in Results and 36% in the TL;DR, and the Introduction says '~1.85 times more effective than top-down', which conflicts with both.

rows.subject: Qwen 1.5 500M
rows.operation_detail: Combined hybrid steering; subtraction of the refusal direction plus harmful-feature steering, with variants not disaggregated.
rows.measure: Relative effectiveness at eliciting harmful responses.
rows.value: 85% relative improvement for harmful instructions only.
rows.note: The text does not give an absolute harmful-response rate or specify the metric behind this relative improvement.
rows.check: This is a hybrid-versus-top-down method comparison, and the evaluation is already on harmful prompts. The meaning of '85% for harmful instructions only' is unclear and conflicts with the 35% figure. It is not a measure of the V1 effect.

rows.subject: Qwen 1.5 500M
rows.operation_detail: Hybrid intervention combining refusal-direction subtraction and harmful-feature addition.
rows.value: A small cost in benign capabilities is reported.
rows.note: No capability metric or magnitude is provided, and this result is for the combined intervention rather than direction removal alone.
rows.check: This is a benign-capability cost of the hybrid intervention, not of direction ablation alone. No metric or magnitude is given.

rows.subject: Qwen 1.5 500M
rows.operation_detail: Subtracts an SAE-reconstructed activation-space refusal direction derived from harmful and harmless prompts.
rows.measure: Effectiveness at bypassing refusal according to string matching.
rows.baseline: Top-down steering; exact comparison value not stated
rows.value: The SAE-reconstructed direction is described as more effective under the string-matching heuristic.
rows.note: The text says the relative ranking is surprising and distinguishes this heuristic result from HarmBench results, where SAE-based methods lose coherence and performance.
rows.check: The direction here is SAE-reconstructed, not the raw difference-in-means direction. The result is a qualitative ranking against other methods under string matching, with no value or unsteered baseline. It is a method comparison.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Top-down mean-difference direction removal on Qwen 1.5 500M, evaluated with HarmBench
reader_labels.reason: The study reports greater harmful-response steering effectiveness than bottom-up SAE steering after subtracting the direction (r1), though it gives only a relative comparison.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Hybrid steering and benign-prompt outcomes on Qwen 1.5 500M
reader_labels.reason: The hybrid improves on top-down steering but combines interventions, and the study reports a small benign-capability cost; neither result establishes that direction removal alone fully removes refusal while preserving other abilities (r2, r3, r4).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: SAE-reconstructed direction evaluated with string matching
reader_labels.reason: The reported direction-method comparison changes with the evaluation measure: the SAE-reconstructed direction is more effective under string matching, while SAE-based methods perform poorly under HarmBench (r5).
